blocks.x: Core definitions
Straight line A straight line can be formed by joining two points, say (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂), where x₁ and x₂ are the x-coordinates (abscissa) and y₁ and y₂ are the y-coordinates (ordinates).

Gradient (slope) The gradient of a line is a measure of how steep the line is and the direction in which it tilts — the ratio of the vertical change to the horizontal change between two points on the line: m = ΔyΔx.

Parallel & perpendicular lines Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient (m₁=m₂). Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is −1 (m₁m₂=−1), equivalently the angle between them is 90°.
Two Points→ Distance / Midpoint→ Gradient→ Equation of Line→ Intersections→ Angle / Distance

sections.title: Length of a straight line (distance between two points)

blocks.x: Two points, one line
If A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂) are any two points, we can find both how far apart they are and the point exactly between them.
Length of a straight line (distance between two points)

|AB| = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) = √((Δx)² + (Δy)²)
or equivalently |AB| = √((x₁−x₂)² + (y₁−y₂)²)
Example: Find the length of the line joining the points A(1, 3) and B(4, 7).

items: 1Write down the distance formula.|AB| = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²)
3Simplify the differences and square them.|AB| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9+16)
4Add and take the square root.|AB| = √25

blocks.x: |AB| = 5 units
Distances to practise
Mid-point of a line segment

If A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂) are any two points on a line, the coordinates of the midpoint M of AB are given by:
M = ( x₁+x₂2, y₁+y₂2 )
Example: Find the midpoint, M, of the line joining A(4, 6) and B(9, 5).

items: 1Write down the midpoint formula.M = ( ½(x₁+x₂), ½(y₁+y₂) )
2Substitute A(4,6) and B(9,5).M = ( ½(4+9), ½(6+5) )
3Add inside each bracket.M = ( ½(13), ½(11) )

sections.title: Gradient of a line joining two points

blocks.x: Steepness, direction, rule
The gradient tells us how steep a line is and which way it tilts; once we know it (plus one point) we can write down the line's full equation.
Gradient of a line joining two points

If A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂) are any two points, the gradient/slope of AB is:
m = y₁−y₂x₁−x₂ = y₂−y₁x₂−x₁ = ΔyΔx
Example: Find the gradient of the line which passes through the points P(1, 1) and Q(7, 2).

items: 1Write down the gradient formula.m = (y₁−y₂)/(x₁−x₂) = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)
3Simplify both forms — they must agree.m = 1/6 = −1/−6

blocks.title: What a gradient means in practice

items: Rate of change: in real life the gradient represents how one quantity changes in relation to another, e.g. speed on a distance-time graph.
Steepness: a larger gradient (in absolute value) means a steeper line; zero gradient means a flat (horizontal) line; an infinite (undefined) gradient signifies a vertical line.

Direction: a positive gradient means the line rises left to right (a road with gradient 2 rises 2 m vertically for every 1 m moved horizontally); a negative gradient means the line falls left to right (a gradient of −1 means the road drops 1 m for every 1 m moved horizontally).

blocks.x: Equation of a straight line

The equation of a straight line is given by y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the intercept on the y-axis. For example, 2x + 4y = 3 is the equation of a line with gradient −12 and y-intercept 34.
The equation can be obtained in two situations:

items: 1Gradient and a point are given: let m be the gradient and (x₁,y₁) the given point. Then y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
2Two points are given: A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂). Then y−y₁=m(x−x₁) or y−y₂=m(x−x₂), where m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁).

blocks.x: Example: Find the equation of the line with m = 3, passing through the point (0, 1).

items: 1Use the point-gradient form with m=3 and (x₁,y₁)=(0,1).y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
2Substitute the values.y − 1 = 3(x − 0)
3Simplify.y − 1 = 3x

blocks.x: Example: Find the equation of the line that passes through A(2, 3) and B(3, 6).

items: 1Find the gradient from the two points.m = (3−6)/(2−3) = (−3)/(−1) = 3
2Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with A(2,3).y − 3 = 3(x − 2)
3Expand and simplify.y − 3 = 3x − 6

blocks.x: How lines relate to each other
Two lines can cross at a single point, run alongside each other forever, or meet at a perfect right angle — each case has its own simple test.
Intersection of lines
If two lines intersect, the coordinates of the point of intersection must satisfy both equations — so the point is found by solving the two equations simultaneously.
Example: Find the point of intersection of the lines 2x − 3y = 8 and 3x + 4y = −5.

items: 1Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 3, so the y-coefficients match.8x − 12y = 32 and 9x + 12y = −15
2Add the two equations to eliminate y.17x = 17 ⇒ x = 1
3Substitute x=1 back into 2x − 3y = 8.2(1) − 3y = 8 ⇒ −3y = 6 ⇒ y = −2

blocks.x: Point of intersection = (1, −2)
Parallel and perpendicular lines
Parallel — two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient, i.e. m₁ = m₂.
Perpendicular — two lines are perpendicular if the gradient of one is the negative reciprocal of the other: m₁ = −1/m₂ (or m₁m₂ = −1). Equivalently, the angle between them is 90°.
Example: Show that l₁: 2y − x = 1 and l₂: 4y = 2x − 8 are parallel.

items: 1Rearrange l₁ into y = mx + c form.2y = x + 1 ⇒ y = ½x + ½ ⇒ m₁ = ½
2Rearrange l₂ into y = mx + c form.4y = 2x − 8 ⇒ y = ½x − 2 ⇒ m₂ = ½

blocks.x: m₁ = m₂ = ½, so l₁ and l₂ are parallel.
Lines with fixed direction

c: Zero gradient; parallel to the x-axis, perpendicular to the y-axis
Infinite (undefined) gradient; parallel to the y-axis, perpendicular to the x-axis

sections.title: The acute angle between two lines

blocks.x: Angles and perpendicular distance
Beyond intersecting, two lines meet at a specific acute angle — and any point off a line has a well-defined shortest (perpendicular) distance to it.
The acute angle between two lines

If two lines with gradients m₁ and m₂ meet at an angle θ, then (taking m₂ > m₁):
tanθ = m₂ − m₁1 + m₂m₁ and if m₁ > m₂, tanθ = m₁ − m₂1 + m₁m₂
Example: Find the angle between the lines 2x − y = 4 and x − y = 3.

items: 1Find each line's gradient.2x−y=4 ⇒ y=2x−4, m₁=2 x−y=3 ⇒ y=x−3, m₂=1
2Since m₁ > m₂, use tanθ = (m₁−m₂)/(1+m₁m₂).tanθ = (2−1)/(1+2×1) = 1/3
3Take arctan of both sides.θ = tan⁻¹(1/3)

blocks.x: Distance from a point to a line

The perpendicular (shortest) distance from a point P₁(x₁,y₁) to the line ax+by+c=0 is:
d = ± ax₁ + by₁ + c√(a²+b²)
Remark (sign convention) If P₁ lies above the line ax+by+c=0, then d is positive. If P₁ lies below the line, then d is negative.
Example: Find the perpendicular distance from the point P(2, 3) to the line 3x + 4y = 5.

items: 1Write the line in the form ax+by+c=0.3x + 4y − 5 = 0 ⇒ a=3, b=4, c=−5
2Substitute P(2,3) into the distance formula.d = (3(2) + 4(3) − 5) / √(3²+4²)
3Simplify numerator and denominator.d = (6 + 12 − 5) / √25 = 13/5

blocks.x: d = 13/5 = 2.6 units
Example: Find the distance from the point P(3, 2) to the line L: 3x − 4y + 4 = 0.

items: 1Identify a, b, c from the line.a=3, b=−4, c=4
2Substitute P(3,2) into d = (ax₁+by₁+c)/√(a²+b²).d = (3(3) − 4(2) + 4) / √(3²+4²)

blocks.x: d = 1 unit
